original_question: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of generalized fatigue, low-grade fever, and a 10-kg (22-lb) weight loss. Physical examination shows generalized pallor and splenomegaly. Her hemoglobin concentration is 7.5 g/dL and leukocyte count is 41,800/mm3. Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase activity is low. Peripheral blood smear shows basophilia with myelocytes and metamyelocytes. Bone marrow biopsy shows cellular hyperplasia with proliferation of immature granulocytic cells. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
ground_truth: Unregulated expression of the ABL1 gene

base.stage_1: A 52-year-old woman presents to the clinic complaining of generalized fatigue that has been ongoing for the past 6 months.
base.stage_2: On physical examination, the patient appears pale and has an enlarged spleen. Her vital signs are stable, but she reports intermittent low-grade fevers.
base.stage_3: Laboratory studies reveal a hemoglobin concentration of 7.5 g/dL and a leukocyte count of 41,800/mm3. Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase activity is noted to be low. A peripheral blood smear demonstrates basophilia along with the presence of myelocytes and metamyelocytes.
base.stage_4: Bone marrow biopsy confirms cellular hyperplasia with a marked proliferation of immature granulocytic cells. Further cytogenetic analysis reveals the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome.

counterfactuals.alteration_description: The absence of splenomegaly makes CML less likely, as it is a common finding due to extramedullary hematopoiesis.
counterfactuals.rules_out: Unregulated expression of the ABL1 gene
